1.explanation: Both prism-fsharp.js and its minified counterpart define the F# language grammar in Prism, including the regular expression that matches F# comments of the form "(* ... *)". Because the current pattern unconditionally treats any "(* ... *)" as a comment, it misclassifies the operator-as-function syntax "(*)" (which is not a comment) as an empty comment. To fix the highlighting bug, those files (the F# language definition) must be updated to distinguish an operator-call "(*)" from a comment delimiter.
1.bug_scenario: In the F# snippet shown, the idiomatic conversion of the multiplication operator into a function (using (*) ) is being mis-highlighted by Prism’s F# syntax highlighter. Prism treats every "(* ... *)" pair as a multi-line comment—so when you write "|> (*) (int cat)", the parser sees the "(*" from your operator function notation and the next ")" as the closing of a comment, and highlights the entire expression as a comment instead of recognizing it as a function call.

2.explanation: The bug stems from the F# language definition in prism-fsharp.js (and its minified counterpart). In that file the regex for F# block comments uses a pattern like /\(\*[\s\S]*?\*\)/ to match nested comments. This pattern doesn’t distinguish the section operator syntax '(*)' from the comment opener '(*', so any use of '(*' as an operator is treated as a comment. To fix this, the comment regex in prism-fsharp.js must be refined (for example, by requiring a non-word boundary or lookbehind) so it only matches actual comments and not the operator form.
2.bug_scenario: When highlighting F# code that uses the sectioned multiplier operator syntax (*) (wrapped in parentheses to convert the infix operator into a function), Prism’s F# highlighter misinterprets "(*" as the start of a block comment. In the user’s snippet the expression "|> (*) (int cat)" causes Prism to think a multiline comment begins at "(*" and it highlights everything that follows as a comment.
